newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong's Tung dines provisional legislature.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong's Tung dines provisional legislature.

text.p: Hong Kong's first post-colonial leader got on with the task of wooing his future team on Monday by dining members of the controversial legislature to be installed when the British colony reverts to China next year.

With only 183 days left until the handover, Tung Chee-hwa is moving quickly to assemble a cabinet and to hammer out his relationship with a provisional legislature China created earlier this month to replace the existing elected chamber upon the transfer. Having secured agreement over the weekend from Hong Kong's influential and popular chief civil servant Anson Chan that she would serve beyond the transition, the 59-year-old Chief Executive-designate scheduled a lunch on Monday for members of the controversial provisional legislature.
Tung said he would this week meet the powerful heads of department of Hong Kong's civil service, the driving force behind the running of the territory of six million people.
He would then select the key members of his future administration and report his decision to Beijing.
British influence is waning dramatically in the countdown to the end of more than 150 years of colonial rule at midnight on June 30, 1997 when Hong Kong reverts to China.
The main topic of discussion at what Tung described as an informal lunchtime meeting on Monday was expected to focus on who would chair the future chamber.

"I'm asking for this lunchtime gathering firstly to congratulate them for becoming members of the provisional legislature and secondly to welcome in the New Year and thirdly just to chat informally as to the challenges ahead and it should be very useful and helpful to everybody," Tung told reporters.
The emphasis was on the informal nature of the meeting.
Tung and the 60 members of the Provisional Legislative Council, chosen by a 400-strong caucus of Hong Kong people carefully vetted by China, are treading a legal tightrope.
"There is no way they can treat themselves as a legislature while we still have a Legislative Council and before the 1st of July 1997," said Gladys Li, head of the Bar Association.
Opponents of the provisional legislature have seized on the argument that it has no constitutional right to act before Britain relinquishes sovereignty over its last Asian outpost.
They argue the existence of a shadow legislature may cripple Hong Kong's law-making body in the countdown to the handover and have threatened to challenge its legality in court.
As a result, the chamber is expected to convene formal meetings across the border in China.
The strongest opposition comes from Hong Kong's largest party, the Democratic Party, who will be kicked out of office when the current legislature is dissolved by China.
Beijing's aim is to undo democratic reforms spearheaded by the last British governor of Hong Kong, Chris Patten.
The party fared the best in last year's elections, when more than one million people voted in the first polls held under the auspices of Patten reforms which enlarged the franchise.
Ten members of pro-Beijing parties defeated in those polls were appointed to the provisional legislature.

Tung, who at the time of the reforms was a member of Patten's inner cabinet of advisers, the Executive Council, has urged the outgoing colonial government to reconsider its refusal to cooperate with the provisional legislature without success.

But he also promised to respect the neutrality of Hong Kong's 180,000 civil servants by refraining from asking them to declare their stance on the legislature, a move welcomed by civil servants worried about potential conflicts of interest.
